Team-authored code lives entirely in C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/FTC_2026_2027/TeamCode/src/main/java/org/firstinspires/ftc/teamcode/ — 45 files, ~14,000 lines. TeamCode/lib contains only OpModeAnnotationProcessor.jar (SDK tooling, not source). The one large file that is NOT team-authored is pedroPathing/Tuning.java (1792 lines, @author Baron Henderson, vendored Pedro tuning menu).
summary: This repo is the opposite of thin: outside the stock SDK it is ~14k lines of dense, hand-written, heavily-Javadoc'd FTC code with a real architecture — a `Superstructure` mode state machine, one class per mechanism, a single 1156-line `RobotConstants`, a Limelight vision layer, Pedro Pathing autos with AprilTag pose correction, and five interchangeable shooter templates. Critically, the README and nearly every util class say outright that these abstractions were **ported FROM the author's FRC template** (`0000-XXXX-Robot-Template`): `AllianceFlipUtil`, `InterpolatingTable`, `AimingCalculator`, `RobotState`, `Superstructure`, `Sensors` all carry an explicit "Ported from the FRC template's X.java" section. So for a new FRC library, most of what's here is a *round trip*, not new material. What IS genuinely new and worth pulling back into FRC is the hardware-resilience layer (`SafeHardware` + `isAvailable()` on every mechanism + an init-time health report), the explicit once-per-loop input caching discipline (`BulkReads` + cached interlock samples in `Superstructure.update()`), the dead-man manual-control pattern in `Climber`, the single-chokepoint soft-limit helper repeated in `Turret`/`Climber`/`Elevator`, and an unusually valuable corpus of ~15 in-code post-mortems marked `*** BUG THAT WAS FIXED HERE ***` that read as a spec for footguns a library should make structurally impossible. The cost side is equally clear: the same ~120 lines of null-guard/ticks-conversion/soft-limit/homing/stall boilerplate is retyped in six mechanisms, the five shooters duplicate an identical spin-up→feed→retract state machine and an identical hardcoded RPM table, and every tuning value is a Java constant requiring a rebuild-and-redeploy.
stack: FTC SDK 11.1.0 (`org.firstinspires.ftc:RobotCore/Hardware/Vision/FtcCommon:11.1.0`), Pedro Pathing `com.pedropathing:ftc:2.1.2` + `com.pedropathing:telemetry:1.0.0`, Panels `com.bylazar:fullpanels:1.0.12` (custom maven `https://mymaven.bylazar.com/releases`). Java 8 only — `build.common.gradle` pins `sourceCompatibility/targetCompatibility JavaVersion.VERSION_1_8`, and `AimingCalculator.ShotSolution` comments "Newer Java has `record` for exactly this, but FTC still compiles against Java 8, so we write it out." AGP 8.7.0, compileSdk 34, minSdk 24, targetSdk 28. Hardware: REV Control Hub (built-in IMU via `RevHubOrientationOnRobot`), goBILDA 5203 Yellow Jacket motors (537.7 ticks/rev) + bare REV HD Hex (28 ticks/rev) for flywheels, `DcMotorEx` everywhere current/velocity is needed, plain `Servo` for feeders/hood/pivot/Blinkin, `DistanceSensor`/`TouchSensor`/`LED`, Limelight 3A configured as an Ethernet Device. No vendordeps/*.json (FTC uses plain Gradle deps), no .vscode, no CLAUDE.md, no swerve config, no PathPlanner, no tuner-project.json, no unit tests, no simulation.
constraints: Java 8 source level is hard-pinned in build.common.gradle — no records, no var, no switch expressions, no sealed types. Any shared library that must also compile for FTC has to be Java 8-clean; an FRC-only library (Java 17) can use records, but the FTC port would then need a parallel hand-written version, exactly as AimingCalculator.ShotSolution shows.

Hardware is discovered by string name at runtime, not constructed by ID — `SafeHardware.tryGet(hardwareMap, DcMotorEx.class, name)` with `name == null` meaning 'this robot does not have this part'. Any config abstraction must support 'device is legitimately absent' as a first-class state, not an error.

Two-step encoder reset is mandatory and easy to get wrong: `setMode(STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER)` then immediately `setMode(RUN_USING_ENCODER)`, or the motor silently refuses power. Called out in readme.md and repeated verbatim in Elevator.init, Turret.init, Climber.init.

Nothing may block: `readme.md` states 'Never use sleep() inside loop()'. Every multi-step action must be a call-me-every-loop state machine (Elevator.updateHoming, SingleShooter.update, Indexer.update, VisionCorrectedAuto.autonomousPathUpdate).

Loop budget is ~20 ms and every encoder/I2C read is a 1-3 ms bus round trip. BulkReads.java documents that the competition TeleOp does 10+ encoder reads per loop; the fix (MANUAL bulk caching) is fragile — 'forgetting to call clearCache freezes every sensor reading forever'.

Units are inches / degrees / seconds / RPM throughout FTC, versus meters / radians in the FRC template — AimingCalculator says so explicitly ('The FRC version uses metres and radians, matching WPILib'). Any shared math library needs an explicit unit boundary rather than bare doubles.

Three mutually incompatible field coordinate frames coexist: Limelight/FIRST (origin at field center, ±72 in), Pedro Pathing (origin at a corner, 0-144 in, rotated a quarter turn), and raw IMU yaw (zeroed wherever the robot faced at INIT). RobotConstants.VisionConstants documents the conversion as `pedroX = ftcY + 72; pedroY = -ftcX + 72` plus a 90-degree yaw offset.

Game-specific values must be isolatable and unknown until kickoff — every unknown is tagged `[KICKOFF]` inside RobotConstants.VisionConstants (tag IDs, goal heights, ball color, mirror axis) so the logic never needs editing.

The project must run on a half-built robot: readme.md promises 'a chassis with nothing but four drive motors runs every OpMode in the project', and every Test OpMode is expected to work with only its one mechanism configured.
No simulation exists and none is possible on the FTC side — all validation is on physical hardware, which is why the Test OpModes and the `[MEASURE THIS]` markers carry so much weight.

patterns.name: SafeHardware — non-throwing hardware lookup + global missing-device registry + init health report
patterns.whatItDoes: Generic `tryGet` wraps `hardwareMap.get()` in try/catch and returns null instead of throwing; a null name is treated as 'not fitted' and deliberately NOT recorded as missing. A static list accumulates every device that failed, and `reportHealth(telemetry)` prints a degraded-mode banner at init. Every mechanism then exposes `isAvailable()` and makes every public method a safe no-op when false.
patterns.whereSeen: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/FTC_2026_2027/TeamCode/src/main/java/org/firstinspires/ftc/teamcode/util/SafeHardware.java (all 140 lines); used in MecanumDrive.init, Elevator.init, Turret.init, Climber.init, Indexer.init, Intake.init, Flywheel.init, Hood.init, StatusLEDs.init, LimelightVision.init; reported in BioBuzzCompetition.init line 92
patterns.libraryValue: This is the single most transferable idea in the repo and it has no WPILib equivalent. FRC's failure mode is different in shape (CAN devices construct fine and then silently return stale/zero data) but identical in consequence, and teams handle it worse: a disconnected Falcon usually produces a mechanism that quietly does nothing. A library could own the whole thing — a `Devices` registry that records construction/connection failures, a `HealthReport` published to NT/Elastic at robotInit, and a `Mechanism` base class whose `isAvailable()` gates commands. The subtle detail worth copying exactly: the interlock consumers must treat 'absent' as 'satisfied', not 'waiting' — `Turret.isAtTarget()` returns TRUE when there is no turret specifically so the shoot interlock does not stall forever on a mechanism the robot does not have.

patterns.name: Superstructure — enum mode machine that commands EVERY actuator on EVERY branch
patterns.whatItDoes: A single `RobotMode` enum (IDLE/INTAKING/EJECTING/AIMING/SHOOTING/SCORING/CLIMB_READY/CLIMBING/MANUAL) owns all nine mechanisms. `update(heading)` does a fixed four-phase cycle: refresh hardware-reading subsystems, sample interlock inputs once, run automatic transitions, then `applyMode()` drives every mechanism. Setting the mode is the entire external interface; TeleOp sets it from buttons and autonomous from its path state machine.
patterns.libraryValue: The interesting content is not the state machine, it is the invariant discovered by breaking it. Three separate documented bugs are all the same defect: a mode that failed to command an actuator left that actuator LATCHED at whatever the previous mode set. `INTAKING`/`EJECTING`/`SCORING`/`CLIMBING` didn't command the turret, so switching out of `AIMING` mid-track left it turning into its travel limit; `MANUAL` didn't stop the intake/indexer/flywheel, so 'all automation off' actually meant 'automation frozen mid-action'. WPILib command-based only partially prevents this via default commands and requirements, and teams that write a superstructure state machine on top of it lose that protection entirely. A library could enforce completeness structurally: a mode returns a map of subsystem→setpoint and the framework applies a declared safe default to every subsystem the map omits, so 'forgot to command it' becomes impossible rather than a comment.

patterns.name: Once-per-loop input cache, applied at three levels
patterns.whatItDoes: Three layered caching disciplines, each added after a measured loop-time problem. (1) `BulkReads` puts every LynxModule in MANUAL bulk-caching mode and requires `clearCache(hubs)` as the literal first line of `loop()`. (2) `Indexer.update()` reads both distance sensors and motor current into `cachedEntryMm/cachedExitMm/cachedCurrentAmps` and every getter serves from the cache. (3) `Superstructure.update()` samples `shooter.isReadyToShoot()` and `turret.isAtTarget()` into per-loop fields so the interlock, the LEDs, and telemetry all read the same values.
patterns.whereSeen: util/BulkReads.java; mechanisms/indexer/Indexer.java lines 100-106 and 162-179; Superstructure.java lines 101-104, 166-172, 356-359; entry point at robots/biobuzz/BioBuzzCompetition.java lines 84 and 109
patterns.libraryValue: This is AdvantageKit's IO-inputs pattern independently rediscovered from first principles, and the comments give the two reasons that matter: cost ('one loop of a test OpMode performed five I2C reads — a quarter of the whole 20 ms loop budget') AND consistency ('the interlock, LEDs and telemetry all agree'). An FRC library should make the consistency argument first-class, not just the performance one: a `Superstructure` that asks `isReadyToShoot()` three times in a loop can get three different answers across a signal refresh boundary, and the resulting bug looks like a flaky shooter. Codifying 'sample once at the top of the cycle into an immutable snapshot, then decide' — even for teams not using AdvantageKit — is worth a small `@AutoInputs`-style helper.

patterns.name: Dead-man manual control: store the request, apply-and-clear inside update()
patterns.whatItDoes: `Climber.manualControl(power)` does not touch the motor — it only stores `manualPower` and sets mode MANUAL. `update()` is the sole place power reaches the motor: it applies `limitAtTravelEnds(manualPower, getHeightInches())` then zeroes `manualPower`. If the OpMode stops calling `manualControl()`, output decays to zero within one ~20 ms loop.
patterns.libraryValue: The bug comment explains why this matters and it applies verbatim to FRC: `setPower`/`set()` LATCHES, so a manual-control method that writes the motor directly keeps winching at the last commanded power forever if the caller stops calling — and the soft limits were only checked at the moment the stick moved, not at the position reached since. WPILib partly mitigates this with the motor safety watchdog and default commands, but hand-rolled manual overrides on climbers and elevators (which every team writes) reintroduce it. A library primitive — `DeadManOutput` / `TimedLatch` that decays to a safe value after N ms without a fresh write, with the limit check re-evaluated at apply time rather than command time — is small, generic, and prevents a genuinely dangerous failure.

patterns.name: Single-chokepoint soft limit that allows escape toward the middle
patterns.whatItDoes: One private method per mechanism zeroes power that would push past a travel end, while still allowing motion back toward center. Every control path in the class — vision tracking, closed-loop angle hold, and manual — routes through it, so a newly added control mode cannot skip the check.
patterns.whereSeen: mechanisms/turret/Turret.java `limitPowerAtTravelEnds` lines 276-284 (used by applyTrackingPower, goToAngle, manualControl); mechanisms/climber/Climber.java `limitAtTravelEnds` lines 254-262 (used by driveToward and the MANUAL case); mechanisms/elevator/Elevator.java lines 148-171 inlines the same logic plus a limit-switch override
patterns.libraryValue: Two design details deserve to be library defaults rather than rediscovered per team: (a) an asymmetric limit — never block the direction that recovers — because symmetric clamping traps a mechanism at its limit with no way out, and (b) a single choke point so limits are structurally unskippable. Elevator additionally shows the right precedence: a physical limit switch overrides the encoder ('encoders can drift; a switch is ground truth') and re-zeros — but only when drift exceeds 0.25 in, because the naive version re-ran `STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER` (two bus writes) every loop the operator held the stick down. That's exactly the kind of detail a shared `SoftLimitedMechanism`/`LimitSwitchHoming` abstraction should bake in.

patterns.name: InterpolatingTable + distance-keyed lookup for RPM, hood angle and flight time
patterns.whatItDoes: A `TreeMap<Double,Double>` with `floorEntry`/`ceilingEntry` lerp, deliberately CLAMPING at the ends rather than extrapolating ('extrapolating past your data means guessing, and a wrong guess here means a flywheel command far outside anything you have tested'), returning 0.0 on an empty table, and exposing `isEmpty()`/`size()` so consumers can detect the silent-failure case.
patterns.whereSeen: util/InterpolatingTable.java (152 lines); consumed by mechanisms/shooter/Flywheel.java (`rpmForDistance`, `loadDefaultRpmTable`), mechanisms/shooter/Hood.java (`angleForDistance`, `loadDefaultAngleTable`), and util/AimingCalculator.java (three tables injected via constructor)
patterns.libraryValue: The class itself is a reimplementation of WPILib's `InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap` (the Javadoc says so), so FRC gains nothing from the data structure. What FRC's version LACKS and this one has are the safety affordances: clamp-not-extrapolate as an explicit documented policy, `isEmpty()` surfaced so an unpopulated table is a detectable fault rather than 'shooter commands 0 RPM and the ball drops on the floor', and `addDataPoint()` designed for live capture from a test routine. A library wrapper — `ShotTable` with validity, provenance, and a live-capture hook feeding a persisted file — is a real improvement over the raw WPILib map.

patterns.name: Vision pose correction with rate limit, outlier gate, blend, and consistent-rejection recovery
patterns.whatItDoes: Wraps a Pedro `Follower`. Rate-limits corrections (0.5 s), rejects poses disagreeing with odometry by more than 24 in, otherwise blends 20% toward vision leaving heading untouched. The novel part: it counts consecutive REJECTIONS that agree with each other within 6 in — three in a row means odometry is the thing that jumped (collision, wheel slip), so it snaps fully to vision instead of locking vision out forever. The vision layer upstream independently gates on tag count (>=2), average tag distance (<=120 in), `isValid()`, and staleness (<=250 ms).
patterns.whereSeen: vision/VisionPoseCorrector.java lines 155-273; quality gates in vision/LimelightVision.java lines 140-177 (update) and 473-498 (getRobotPoseInches); constants in RobotConstants.VisionConstants lines 718-806; driven from pedroPathing/VisionCorrectedAuto.java
patterns.libraryValue: WPILib's `SwerveDrivePoseEstimator` covers blending via std-devs, but almost every FRC team writes the outlier gate by hand and virtually all of them write the version with the bug documented here: reject-forever, which disables vision at exactly the moment a collision made it most necessary. The consistent-rejection escape hatch is a genuinely good idea and is not in WPILib. Equally worth lifting are the diagnostics the class exposes for the drive team — `getCorrectionsApplied()`, `getCorrectionsRejected()`, `getLastCorrectionInches()` — with the comment 'If this stays at 0 through a whole autonomous, vision correction is not actually doing anything and you are running on odometry without realizing it.' A library `VisionGate` that publishes accept/reject counters and reject reasons would catch a very common silent failure.

patterns.name: Derived-constant discipline: declare physical facts, compute conversions
patterns.whatItDoes: Gearing constants are never typed as a final number. Ticks-per-motor-rev, gear ratio and spool/drum diameter are declared separately and the conversion is computed in the constants class itself.
patterns.whereSeen: RobotConstants.java: ElevatorConstants lines 206-222 (TICKS_PER_INCH), ClimberConstants lines 478-488, TurretConstants lines 835-846 (TICKS_PER_DEGREE), ShooterConstants lines 973-984 (DRUM_TICKS_PER_REV, DRUM_TICKS_PER_SLOT)
patterns.libraryValue: The rationale ('swap to a different spool, change one number above, everything else stays correct — typing the final number in yourself is how unit bugs get created') is exactly the argument for a typed gearing/mechanism-config object in an FRC library: `LinearMechanismConfig(motorTicksPerRev, gearRatio, drumDiameter)` producing `Distance <-> Rotations` converters, and `RotaryMechanismConfig` doing the same for the turret. Combined with a units type this eliminates a whole bug class. Note the FTC code stops one step short: the conversion is centralized but the *result* is still a bare double, so `Elevator.inchesToTicks` and `Turret` divide-by-TICKS_PER_DEGREE are still hand-written per mechanism.

patterns.name: In-code post-mortem convention: `*** BUG THAT WAS FIXED HERE ***`
patterns.whatItDoes: Roughly fifteen fixed defects are documented in place with the symptom, why it survived testing, and the generalizable lesson. Git history confirms them: commit cc56e22 'Fix 35 defects found by multi-agent adversarial code review'.
patterns.whereSeen: MecanumDrive.java lines 184-190 (mixing signs) and 305-318 (field-centric rotation); AutoAlign.java lines 141-147 (strafe projected onto LEFT while drive() is RIGHT-positive); AimingCalculator.java lines 188-195 (turret CCW vs CW); Indexer.java lines 211-221 (time-window counted one ball 3x) and 337-343 (re-entrant unjam reversed forever) and 461-467; Superstructure.java lines 108-114, 220-225, 301-308, 393-399; VisionPoseCorrector.java lines 180-188 and 255-269 (Pedro/FTC frame rotation); pedroPathing/Constants.java lines 37-56 (Follower built with null drivetrain and localizer — compiled fine, crashed every auto); VisionCorrectedAuto.java lines 109-114 and 122-133; BioBuzzCompetition.java lines 214-224 and 237-243
patterns.libraryValue: Treat this list as the requirements document for the library rather than as a pattern to copy. Five of the fifteen are sign/frame convention errors at a module boundary (CW vs CCW turret, strafe left vs right, field-centric rotation direction, Pedro vs FTC axes, IMU yaw vs field yaw) — every one of which a typed `Rotation2d`/`ChassisSpeeds`-style API or an explicit `FieldFrame`/`RobotFrame` marker type makes unrepresentable. Three are latched-actuator bugs. Two are edge-detection/debounce bugs (a time window instead of a consumed flag). Two are lifecycle/ordering bugs (`SafeHardware.resetMissingDevices()` called inside a participant erased the drivetrain's registrations; the Limelight not started before `init_loop` read it). One — `pedroPathing/Constants.java` — is a builder that compiled cleanly with two required stages omitted, producing null internals and crashing all four autos, which is a direct argument for required-stage typed builders over fluent optional setters.

painPoints.problem: The same ~120-line mechanism skeleton is retyped in six classes: null-guard every public method, ticks<->units conversion pair, min/max soft limit with escape, homing start/update pair against an optional switch, encoder-reset two-step, and stall detection.
painPoints.evidence: Elevator.java (422 lines), Turret.java (398), Climber.java (432), Indexer.java (596), Flywheel.java (274) and DrumShooter.java (500) each independently implement `isAvailable()`, private ticks conversion, a private travel-limit helper, and `resetEncoder()` with the STOP_AND_RESET/RUN_USING two-step. `Elevator.isStalled()` hardcodes its own thresholds inline — `return currentAmps > 5.0 && velocityTicksPerSecond < 10.0;` (Elevator.java:384) — while Indexer uses `IndexerConstants.STALL_CURRENT_AMPS = 6.0` and DualTowerShooter uses `TOWER_STALL_CURRENT_AMPS = 6.0`. Three stall detectors, three thresholds, one of them a magic number outside the constants file.
painPoints.libraryFix: A `PositionMechanism` base (or composable `Mechanism` + `SoftLimits` + `Homing` + `StallDetector` pieces) that takes a gearing config and a limit-switch supplier and provides units-in/units-out, asymmetric soft limits, a non-blocking homing routine, and one stall detector with a single configured threshold. Elevator/Turret/Climber then become ~60 lines of policy each instead of 400 lines of restated plumbing.

painPoints.problem: Five shooter templates duplicate an identical spin-up→feed→retract state machine and an identical hardcoded RPM table, so a fix or a re-tune has to be applied five times.
painPoints.evidence: `loadDefaultRpmTable()` with the exact same five pairs (24→2400, 48→2900, 72→3400, 96→3900, 120→4400) appears in Flywheel.java:141-145 and again in ParallelShooter.java (~line 150), and the other shooters repeat the shape. SingleShooter (280 lines), ParallelShooter (487), DrumShooter (500), RollerShooter (426) and DualTowerShooter (606) each carry their own `ShotState` enum, `ElapsedTime stateTimer`, `shotsFired` counter, and a switch whose FEEDING/RETRACTING branches are structurally identical. SingleShooter composes `Flywheel` but ParallelShooter does not — it manages two motors itself.
painPoints.libraryFix: Factor the timed-sequence part out entirely: a small `TimedSequence`/`Action` primitive (steps with a guard and a duration, advanced by `update()`) plus a reusable `VelocityMechanism` for each wheel. A shooter then declares its steps rather than re-implementing a switch. The RPM table belongs in one shared, externally-loaded `ShotTable` — right now re-tuning the shooter means editing Java in whichever of five files is in use and redeploying.

painPoints.problem: Every tunable number is a compile-time Java constant. Re-tuning at a competition means edit, rebuild, redeploy — the very scenario RobotConstants' own Javadoc says it exists to make fast.
painPoints.evidence: RobotConstants.java is 1156 lines of `public static final`, including all the values readme.md's calibration table says must be measured on the real robot (elevator ticks/inch, preset heights, turret gear ratio, camera height and pitch, indexer detect threshold, drum gear ratio, climber limits). The two lookup tables are hardcoded in Java (`Flywheel.loadDefaultRpmTable`, `Hood.loadDefaultAngleTable`). Panels' `@Configurable` — which would give live tuning — is applied only to the four Pedro autos (PedroPathingAuto_Forward/Strafe/Square, VisionCorrectedAuto) and never to any mechanism or to RobotConstants. The Test OpModes work around this with dpad increment/decrement into a local field (`ShooterTest.java:87-99` adjusts `targetRpm` by 100/25) and then instruct the student to 'Put all your pairs into Flywheel.loadDefaultRpmTable()' — i.e. transcribe by hand and rebuild.
painPoints.libraryFix: A `TunableNumber` that reads a constant by default but overrides from dashboard/NT (or a file) when a tuning-mode flag is set, plus a persisted table format so a shooter table captured live survives a redeploy without a source edit. This is the highest-leverage missing abstraction: the workflow it would replace — dpad-tune, write numbers on paper, retype into Java, rebuild — is the single biggest documented time cost in the repo.

painPoints.problem: A mode/state that forgets to command an actuator leaves it latched at the previous mode's output — three separate shipped bugs, all with the same root cause, all fixed by comment and vigilance rather than structure.
painPoints.evidence: Superstructure.java:220-225 — INTAKING (and EJECTING/SCORING/CLIMBING) never commanded the turret, so leaving AIMING mid-track left it turning into its travel limit. Superstructure.java:301-308 — MANUAL commanded only the three stick-driven mechanisms, so entering MANUAL from SHOOTING left the flywheel at speed and the indexer feeding: 'all automation off was actually automation frozen mid-action, which is worse.' Climber.java:193-207 — the MANUAL case was empty because power had been set elsewhere, so a released stick latched the winch at its last power. The current defence is a repeated hand-written comment: `turret.stop();   // see INTAKING - never leave the turret uncommanded`.
painPoints.libraryFix: Make omission impossible instead of commented. Have a mode produce a declarative setpoint map and let the framework apply a per-subsystem safe default to anything omitted; or give each subsystem a watchdog that reverts to a neutral output if it receives no command in a cycle (the `Climber` dead-man pattern, generalized). Either way the library, not the author's memory, enforces 'every mode commands every actuator.'

painPoints.problem: Sign and coordinate-frame conventions are carried in comments and bare doubles, and five separate shipped bugs came from crossing a frame boundary.
painPoints.evidence: MecanumDrive.java:184-190 (mixing formula had strafe and rotate negated), MecanumDrive.java:305-318 (field-centric rotation written for a left-positive lateral axis while `drive()` is right-positive — 'Worked perfectly at heading 0, which is exactly why it survived bench testing'), AutoAlign.java:141-147 (strafe error projected onto the LEFT unit vector, pushing the robot away from the target), AimingCalculator.java:188-196 (solver was CCW-positive, `Turret` is CW-positive, so every solve aimed the mirror image), VisionPoseCorrector.java:255-269 (Pedro/FTC conversion assumed translation-only when it is a quarter-turn rotation plus a shift — 'every vision correction mapped to a point reflected across the field diagonal - up to ~100 inches wrong'), VisionCorrectedAuto.java:122-133 (raw IMU yaw fed to MegaTag2 instead of field-frame yaw). The frame conversion itself lives as two loose constants: `FIELD_CENTER_OFFSET_INCHES = 72.0` and `PEDRO_TO_FTC_YAW_OFFSET_DEGREES = 90.0`.
painPoints.libraryFix: Types, not comments. Distinct `FieldRelative`/`RobotRelative` wrapper types (or at minimum WPILib `Translation2d`/`Rotation2d`/`ChassisSpeeds` used consistently) so a field-frame error cannot be passed to a robot-frame consumer, plus one `FrameTransform` object owning any external-library conversion with a documented round-trip self-check. The author's own conclusion in AimingCalculator.java:194 — 'Sign conventions at module boundaries deserve as much attention as the math itself' — is the requirement.

painPoints.problem: Manual bulk-cache invalidation is a load-bearing convention with a catastrophic, silent failure mode.
painPoints.evidence: BulkReads.java's own Javadoc: 'forgetting to call clearCache freezes every sensor reading forever, which is the classic bulk-caching bug. Call it first thing in loop().' `BioBuzzCompetition.loop()` line 109 is `BulkReads.clearCache(hubs);` with a comment shouting 'FIRST LINE, every loop'. MANUAL mode was chosen over AUTO deliberately because the codebase reads some encoders more than once per loop — which is itself a consequence of not having a single input-snapshot layer.
painPoints.libraryFix: Own the loop lifecycle in the library so cache invalidation happens in the framework's periodic entry, not the author's first line. The FRC analogue is batched signal refresh (`BaseStatusSignal.refreshAll`) and AdvantageKit's `updateInputs` — a shared `RobotLoop` that begins each cycle by refreshing all registered inputs removes an entire class of stale-sensor bug from user code.

painPoints.problem: Pure, trivially testable logic has zero tests, so every defect had to be found by review or on hardware.
painPoints.evidence: No test source set exists anywhere in TeamCode/build.gradle. `InterpolatingTable`, `AimingCalculator.wrapDegrees`/`solve`, `AllianceFlipUtil.applyX/applyY/applyHeading`, `AutoAlign.driveToPose`, `DriverInput.shape/clamp`, and the mecanum mixing math in `MecanumDrive.drive` are all pure functions with no hardware dependency. Every one of the sign-convention bugs listed above would have been caught by a three-line assertion; instead readme.md's closing line reads 'It compiles ≠ it works ... The whole project compiled cleanly while every single Pedro Pathing autonomous crashed on startup.'
painPoints.libraryFix: Keep the library's math layer hardware-free and ship it with tests, so consumers inherit verified kinematics, angle wrapping, alliance mirroring and interpolation instead of retyping them. The frame-crossing conventions in particular should be pinned by tests (e.g. 'at heading +90, pushing forward strafes robot-right') — the author already wrote exactly that sanity check as a comment in MecanumDrive.java:316-318 but had no place to execute it.

painPoints.problem: Global mutable static state for alliance and robot pose.
painPoints.evidence: `AllianceFlipUtil` holds `private static boolean isRedAlliance` mutated by a static setter (AllianceFlipUtil.java:73-83) and read by static `applyX/applyY/applyHeading`. `RobotState` is a `synchronized` singleton (`getInstance()`, RobotState.java:56-66) holding position and computed velocity; its own Javadoc concedes 'Singletons are worth using sparingly - shared mutable state makes code harder to follow and harder to test.' `Superstructure` separately keeps its own `isBlueAlliance` field, so alliance is stored in two places that can disagree. `SafeHardware.missingDevices` is likewise static, which caused the reset-ordering bug documented at Superstructure.java:108-114.
painPoints.libraryFix: Make alliance an injected value resolved once at init (FRC has `DriverStation.getAlliance()` as the authoritative source) and make pose an explicitly-owned object passed to consumers, or at minimum a single source of truth. The FTC code already pays for the duplication — alliance lives in both `AllianceFlipUtil` and `Superstructure` with no link between them.

painPoints.problem: Servo motion completion is estimated from a timer because FTC servos give no feedback, and this estimate silently participates in the shot interlock.
painPoints.evidence: Hood.java records `lastMoveFraction = Math.abs(clamped - hoodServo.getPosition())` and resets `moveTimer` on every command, then `isAtTarget()` compares elapsed time against `HoodConstants.FULL_TRAVEL_SECONDS = 0.6` scaled by that fraction; Intake.java does the identical thing for its pivot with `PIVOT_TRAVEL_SECONDS = 0.5`. `Superstructure.applyMode()` SHOOTING branch gates firing on `hood.isAtTarget()` — an estimate, not a measurement. Note `hoodServo.getPosition()` returns the last *commanded* position, so the 'current' position it diffs against is itself an assumption.
painPoints.libraryFix: FRC mostly avoids this (servos are rare, and actuators have encoders), so the transferable piece is narrow but real: a `MotionEstimate` type that reports `isAtTarget()` together with its confidence source (measured vs. timed), so an interlock can distinguish 'the hood has arrived' from 'the hood has probably arrived' and a library can refuse to let an estimate silently gate a safety-critical action.

painPoints.problem: Constants organization does not scale past one robot: a single 1156-line file, alphabet-soup naming for variant hardware, and dead sections left in place.
painPoints.evidence: RobotConstants.java holds 13 nested classes in one file. `ShooterConstants` alone spans lines 902-1155 and carries names for all five shooter variants simultaneously (`PARALLEL_LEFT_FLYWHEEL_NAME`, `ROLLER_MOTOR_2_NAME`, `TOWER_A_FEED_NAME`, `TOWER_AGITATOR_NAME`...) even though readme.md says 'build one, delete the rest'. `LauncherConstants` (lines 276-306) is a stale duplicate of `ShooterConstants` with its own `LAUNCHER_MOTOR_NAME`/`FEEDER_SERVO_NAME`/`RPM_CLOSE`/`RPM_FAR` and appears unused by any mechanism. `ShooterConstants` also declares `HOOD_SERVO_NAME` while a separate `HoodConstants` declares `HOOD_SERVO_NAME` again — two sources for the same device.
painPoints.libraryFix: Per-mechanism config objects constructed and passed in (rather than statically reached into), so a robot declares only the mechanisms it has and a variant that isn't built has no constants at all. This also kills the duplicate-name problem structurally: a device name exists once, in the config handed to the mechanism that owns it.
